prompt: Grover gives square-root query growth for unstructured search. If the candidates are all assignments to a growing number of SAT variables, what does this establish?

options.text: A polynomial-time algorithm for every SAT instance
options.explanation: The square root of an exponential candidate count is still exponential.

options.text: A quadratic improvement in black-box queries, with exponential growth remaining
options.explanation: The query exponent is reduced, but no polynomial-time SAT claim follows.

options.text: A proof that quantum computers cannot exploit formula structure
options.explanation: The lower bound concerns black-box search and does not rule out every structured approach.

options.text: A measured quantum runtime equal to the query count
options.explanation: Implementing coherent oracle queries has additional physical and computational cost.

workedExample: Grover reduces the number of black-box queries to a square-root scale. The number of assignments already grows exponentially with variable count, so taking its square root still leaves exponential growth. This proves a query-model improvement, not polynomial-time SAT, and each coherent oracle call also has an implementation cost.

link.title: Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantum Computing — BBBV

prompt: A news article makes several claims about quantum computing. Which are accurate according to current complexity theory? Select all that apply.

options.text: Quantum computers will solve NP-complete problems like SAT in polynomial time
options.explanation: Not supported. NP inside BQP is widely believed false; black-box methods are limited to Grover's quadratic speed-up, still exponential for SAT (the square root of 2-to-the-n for n variables).

options.text: Grover's quadratic speed-up for unstructured search is the best possible for black-box search
options.explanation: Accurate: Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani (1997) proved that black-box search over N items needs at least a constant times the square root of N queries.

options.text: It has been proven that quantum computers solve some decision problem exponentially faster than any classical algorithm
options.explanation: Not proven. Unconditional separations exist only relative to oracles or in query/communication models. Without them, it would imply P differs from PSPACE.

options.text: Factoring is NP-complete, which is why Shor's algorithm matters
options.explanation: The bounded-factor decision problem is in both NP and coNP and is believed not NP-complete. Shor matters because efficient factoring breaks RSA and efficient discrete logarithms break elliptic-curve schemes.

workedExample: Shor gives polynomial-time factoring and discrete logarithms on the quantum model, including the associated factoring decision problem in BQP. Grover’s square-root query scaling is optimal for black-box search. Neither result puts all NP problems in BQP or proves BPP differs from BQP. The hard part of a separation is ruling out every classical algorithm, not exhibiting one good quantum algorithm.
